lesson.title: Mapping the Heat: How Temperature and Phase Change Together
lesson.summary: A heating curve plots temperature against heat added and shows two distinct behaviors: sloped segments where added heat raises temperature within one phase, and flat plateaus where added heat drives a phase change at constant temperature.
lesson.body:
A heating curve is a graph with heat added, or equivalently, time under constant heating, on the horizontal axis and temperature on the vertical axis, and it is one of the clearest visual summaries of everything covered so far in this unit. As you add heat to a sample steadily, starting as a solid well below its melting point, the graph shows a predictable pattern: temperature rises, then holds flat, then rises again, then holds flat again, then rises once more.

The sloped segments correspond to heating within a single phase, governed by q = mcDeltaT. During these segments, every joule of added energy goes directly into increasing the average kinetic energy of the molecules, which is what temperature measures, so the thermometer reading climbs steadily. The steepness of the slope depends on the specific heat capacity of that phase: a smaller c means temperature rises faster per joule added, so the solid, liquid, and gas phases, which usually have different c values from each other, will show different slopes on the same graph.

The flat plateaus correspond to phase changes: melting and boiling, in the case of a substance being heated from solid to gas. During a plateau, the substance is absorbing heat, but that energy is not increasing average kinetic energy at all. Instead it is being spent entirely on overcoming intermolecular forces, pulling molecules out of a solid lattice or fully separating them into a gas, which is potential energy in the intermolecular sense, not kinetic energy. Since temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, and kinetic energy is not changing during the plateau, temperature does not change either, even though heat is very much still flowing in. This is the same logic behind the plateaus discussed conceptually in the phase changes chapter, now made visible as a literal flat region on a graph. The length of a plateau, how much heat it takes to cross, is proportional to the latent heat of that particular phase change, quantified precisely in the heat of fusion and heat of vaporization chapters that follow.

Consider just the first sloped segment of a heating curve for a 45.0 g sample of liquid water starting at 25.0 C and heating up to its boiling point at 100.0 C. Using q = mcDeltaT with c = 4.184 J/(g C): q = (45.0 g)(4.184 J/g C)(75.0 C) = 14,121 J, about 14.1 kJ. On the graph, this shows up as a straight, upward sloping line from 25.0 C to 100.0 C. The moment the sample hits exactly 100.0 C, the graph flattens into a plateau: additional heat added at that point converts liquid water to steam without pushing the temperature past 100.0 C, until every last drop has vaporized, at which point the line would resume climbing as the now gaseous steam heats further above 100.0 C.
